tracks.title: Foundations
tracks.blurb: The ideas every other track builds on. Start here whatever you write.

lessons.title: The shared core
lessons.subtitle: What nearly every theory agrees on
lessons.summary: Across 2,400 years of argument, almost every theorist agrees that a story is change under pressure: someone wants something, meets resistance, and comes out different.

lessons.title: Aristotle
lessons.subtitle: Poetics, c. 335 BCE
lessons.summary: The first surviving theory of story, and still the one everyone argues with: plot is the soul of drama, and events must follow from each other, not just after each other.

lessons.title: Edgar Allan Poe
lessons.subtitle: The Philosophy of Composition, 1846
lessons.summary: Decide the ending and the single effect you want first, then choose every incident, word and length to produce it, ideally in a piece read at one sitting.

lessons.title: Gustav Freytag
lessons.subtitle: The pyramid, 1863
lessons.summary: A five-act tragedy rises through an exciting force to a climax at its center, then falls through the tragic force and a last flicker of suspense to the catastrophe.

lessons.title: E. M. Forster
lessons.subtitle: Aspects of the Novel, 1927
lessons.summary: Story asks "and then?", plot asks "why?"; and characters are flat, built round one quality, or round, able to surprise us convincingly.

lessons.title: Lajos Egri
lessons.subtitle: The Art of Dramatic Writing, 1946
lessons.summary: Start from a premise and from fully dimensioned characters, and let conflict rise step by step between opponents who can't walk away from each other.

lessons.title: Vladimir Propp
lessons.subtitle: Morphology of the Folktale, 1928
lessons.summary: Hundreds of Russian wonder tales are built from the same 31 acts, or functions, always in the same order, shared among seven roles.

lessons.title: Joseph Campbell & Christopher Vogler
lessons.subtitle: The hero's journey, 1949 and 1992
lessons.summary: Campbell found one pattern of departure, initiation and return beneath the world's hero myths; Vogler turned it into twelve stages and a set of character masks for screenwriters.

lessons.title: Story vs. telling
lessons.subtitle: Shklovsky, Genette and Chatman on the order of events
lessons.summary: Every story exists twice, as events in the order they happened and as a telling with its own order, speed and point of view, and much of the craft lives in the gap.

lessons.title: Janet Burroway
lessons.subtitle: Writing Fiction, 1982
lessons.summary: Only trouble is interesting: a story moves through conflict and crisis to a changed situation, told through significant detail and with its key moments in scene.

lessons.title: Same skeleton, three media
lessons.subtitle: How screen, stage and page bend the core
lessons.summary: The deep rules are shared. What differs is who controls the audience's attention, and whether you invent the events or have to find them.

tracks.title: Screen
tracks.blurb: Film and television, where structure is most codified, partly because the industry buys it that way.

lessons.title: Syd Field
lessons.subtitle: Screenplay, 1979
lessons.summary: A feature film is three acts, setup, confrontation and resolution, in roughly 30, 60 and 30 pages, joined by plot points that spin the story in a new direction.

lessons.title: Robert McKee
lessons.subtitle: Story, 1997
lessons.summary: Every scene must turn a value from positive to negative or back, and the engine of every turn is the gap between what a character expects and what the world does.

lessons.title: John Truby
lessons.subtitle: The Anatomy of Story, 2007
lessons.summary: Structure should grow organically from a hero's change, from weakness and need to self-revelation, with an opponent who fights for the same goal and a moral argument made through action.

lessons.title: Blake Snyder
lessons.subtitle: Save the Cat!, 2005
lessons.summary: Know what your movie is in a logline, give the audience a reason to root for the hero, and hit fifteen beats from Opening Image to its mirror, the Final Image.

lessons.title: Dan Harmon
lessons.subtitle: The story circle
lessons.summary: Every story is a circle: a character leaves comfort to chase a want, gets it in an unfamiliar world, pays a price, and comes home changed, at any scale from a scene to a season.

lessons.title: Frank Daniel & Paul Gulino
lessons.subtitle: The sequence approach
lessons.summary: Break a feature into about eight 10–15 minute sequences, each a little film with its own goal and tension, and the long second act becomes manageable.

lessons.title: Kristin Thompson
lessons.subtitle: Storytelling in the New Hollywood, 1999
lessons.summary: Time real Hollywood films and you find not three acts but four parts of roughly equal length, divided by turning points where the protagonist's goals change.

lessons.title: Dwight Swain
lessons.subtitle: Scene and sequel, 1965
lessons.summary: Stories alternate scenes (goal, conflict, disaster) with sequels (reaction, dilemma, decision), and at the smallest scale every reaction should follow its cause in the order feeling, action, speech.

lessons.title: John Yorke
lessons.subtitle: Into the Woods, 2013
lessons.summary: Every story is a journey into the woods and back, and its five-act shape, hinged on a midpoint, repeats fractally in every act and scene to dramatize a character's change.

lessons.title: David Mamet
lessons.subtitle: On Directing Film, 1991
lessons.summary: Tell the story in the cut, cut the exposition, and ask of every scene: who wants what, what happens if they don't get it, and why now?

lessons.title: Pixar's story rules
lessons.subtitle: Emma Coats, 2011
lessons.summary: A story artist's tweeted notes and an improv teacher's story spine boil story down to cause and effect: one day, because of that, because of that, until finally.

lessons.title: Television structure
lessons.subtitle: Acts, storylines and seasons
lessons.summary: Television structure grew from advertising and the need for stories that never end: act-outs before the breaks, interwoven A, B and C stories, and an engine that generates episodes for years.

tracks.title: Stage
tracks.blurb: Live bodies in one shared space, where words are the action and the audience decides where to look.

lessons.title: The well-made play
lessons.subtitle: Scribe, Sardou and Ibsen
lessons.summary: Scribe and Sardou built plays as suspense machines around a secret and an obligatory scene; Ibsen kept the machinery and turned the ending into discussion, and Shaw mocked the rest as "Sardoodledom".

lessons.title: Anton Chekhov
lessons.subtitle: Indirect action
lessons.summary: Put the big events offstage and show people living around them: in Chekhov the drama is in the subtext, and the famous gun is about economy, not twists.

lessons.title: Konstantin Stanislavski
lessons.subtitle: Objectives and the through-line
lessons.summary: Every character is always trying to do something to someone: tasks build into a through-line toward a super-objective, and a playwright who writes that way gives actors something to play.

lessons.title: Bertolt Brecht
lessons.subtitle: Epic theatre, against Aristotle
lessons.summary: Instead of drawing the audience into a hero's fate, epic theatre makes the familiar strange, with episodes, songs and titles, so the audience asks why things happen and whether they could change.

lessons.title: David Ball
lessons.subtitle: Backwards and Forwards, 1983
lessons.summary: A play is a chain of triggers and heaps from stasis to new stasis; read it backwards to check every link, and forwards to feel what keeps an audience hungry for next.

lessons.title: María Irene Fornés
lessons.subtitle: Playwright and teacher
lessons.summary: A playwright and legendary teacher who built plays from images and characters rather than outlines, and taught writers to begin with the body and the eyes closed.

lessons.title: Paula Vogel
lessons.subtitle: Structure beyond the arc
lessons.summary: The Aristotelian arc is one plot form among several: plays can circle, run backward or repeat, and the form you choose is part of what the play means.

lessons.title: Suzan-Lori Parks
lessons.subtitle: Elements of Style, 1995
lessons.summary: Like a jazz phrase, a line can return again and again, revised each time: Rep & Rev builds meaning by accumulation, scored with rests and spells.

lessons.title: Sarah Ruhl
lessons.subtitle: 100 Essays I Don't Have Time to Write, 2014
lessons.summary: The character arc is one option that has become compulsory; plays can instead take Ovidian pleasure in sudden transformation rather than moral improvement.

tracks.title: Journalism
tracks.blurb: Stories made of facts. You can't invent a better ending, so structure becomes the art of finding and ordering.

lessons.title: The inverted pyramid
lessons.subtitle: News, most important first
lessons.summary: Hard news orders facts by importance, not time or tension: the most important first, so a reader can stop anywhere and an editor can cut from the bottom.

lessons.title: The feature formula
lessons.subtitle: Anecdote, nut graf, kicker
lessons.summary: Open with one person in a vivid moment, pull back in a nut graf to say why it matters, back it up, and end by circling back to where you began.

lessons.title: Jon Franklin
lessons.subtitle: Writing for Story, 1986
lessons.summary: A true story is a complication and its resolution. Find the resolution first, then outline the whole piece in a few short, active statements.

lessons.title: Jack Hart
lessons.subtitle: Storycraft, 2011
lessons.summary: Every story is a narrative, but not every narrative is a story: choose the form your material supports, from a full arc with a point of insight to an explanatory narrative with no resolution at all.

lessons.title: Tom Wolfe & the New Journalism
lessons.subtitle: Fiction's tools for fact, 1973
lessons.summary: Reporters can use the novelist's tools, scene, dialogue, point of view and status detail, but only if saturation reporting stands behind every one.

lessons.title: John McPhee
lessons.subtitle: Draft No. 4, 2017
lessons.summary: Find the structure before you write the first sentence, and find it in the material rather than imposing a template on it.

lessons.title: Vivian Gornick
lessons.subtitle: The Situation and the Story, 2001
lessons.summary: Every piece has a situation, what happened, and a story, what the writer has come to understand, told by a narrator built to be trusted.

lessons.title: Ira Glass
lessons.subtitle: Anecdote and reflection
lessons.summary: Alternate an anecdote, a sequence of actions that pulls the listener forward by raising questions, with a moment of reflection that says why it matters.

lessons.title: Janet Malcolm & John Hersey
lessons.subtitle: The ethics of shaping fact
lessons.summary: Shaping facts into story has limits: the writer must not invent, and must reckon with what the story does to the reader's trust and to the people in it.

tracks.title: Counterpoints
tracks.blurb: Thinkers who question the conflict-driven arc. Know the rules well enough to choose when to break them.

lessons.title: Kishōtenketsu
lessons.subtitle: Four parts, no conflict required
lessons.summary: A four-part pattern from Chinese poetry, Japanese and Korean writing and the four-panel comic: introduce, develop, twist, reconcile, so the turn can be a new perspective rather than a clash.

lessons.title: The Nāṭyaśāstra
lessons.subtitle: Bharata on plot and rasa
lessons.summary: India's founding treatise on drama centers on the audience's experience: rasa, the savored taste of emotion, and a plot that moves through five stages toward the hero's goal.

lessons.title: Zeami
lessons.subtitle: Jo-ha-kyū and the rhythm of Noh
lessons.summary: Noh's great theorist taught that everything on stage, from a gesture to a day of plays, should open slowly, deepen, and close swiftly: jo-ha-kyū.

lessons.title: Ursula K. Le Guin
lessons.subtitle: The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction, 1986
lessons.summary: Fiction needn't be a spear aimed at a climax; it can be a carrier bag that holds people, events and meanings together, with conflict as only one thing inside.

lessons.title: Charles Baxter
lessons.subtitle: Burning Down the House, 1997
lessons.summary: When stories, like public life, say 'mistakes were made', nobody acts; fiction comes alive when characters make choices, get them wrong and own them.

lessons.title: Jane Alison
lessons.subtitle: Meander, Spiral, Explode, 2019
lessons.summary: The arc is one shape among many: stories can ripple, meander, spiral, radiate or explode, and pattern can pull a reader as strongly as suspense.

lessons.title: George Saunders
lessons.subtitle: A Swim in a Pond in the Rain, 2021
lessons.summary: Structure is what a story does to a reader page by page: each section should escalate, and patterns earn their meaning when they bend or break.

lessons.title: Matthew Salesses
lessons.subtitle: Craft in the Real World, 2021
lessons.summary: Craft isn't a set of universal rules but a set of cultural expectations, so writers should name their audience and workshops should make their assumptions explicit.

tracks.title: Lenses & Critiques
tracks.blurb: How stories are received, who they leave out, and the case against narrative itself. Plus comedy and documentary.

lessons.title: Susan Sontag
lessons.subtitle: Against Interpretation, 1964
lessons.summary: Interpretation that translates a work into a hidden meaning can stop us experiencing it; Sontag asked critics, and writers, to attend to form and sensation, and later asked how images of suffering should be framed.

lessons.title: Walter Benjamin
lessons.subtitle: The Storyteller, 1936
lessons.summary: Information is explained and expires once it's no longer new, but a story passes on experience and keeps its force for centuries, precisely because the teller leaves it unexplained.

lessons.title: Roland Barthes
lessons.subtitle: Codes, and the death of the author
lessons.summary: Stories are woven from codes, above all enigmas raised and deliberately delayed and actions we recognize from their first step, and their meaning is made by the reader, not fixed by the author.

lessons.title: Hayden White & Joan Didion
lessons.subtitle: The shape we impose on facts
lessons.summary: Facts don't come with plots: historians and reporters choose whether events become romance, tragedy, comedy or satire, and Didion shows what happens when the stories we live by stop working.

lessons.title: Frank Kermode & Peter Brooks
lessons.subtitle: Why endings matter
lessons.summary: Endings give the middle its meaning: Kermode shows how plot turns mere time into meaningful time between tick and tock, and Brooks how readers are driven forward by desire for the end.

lessons.title: Point of view and voice
lessons.subtitle: Booth, Bakhtin and free indirect style
lessons.summary: Who sees and who speaks shapes everything: a narrator can be trusted or seen through, voices can argue without the author settling it, and third person can slip inside a character's mind.

lessons.title: Who gets to be the subject
lessons.subtitle: Mulvey, Adichie and King
lessons.summary: Every story decides whose desires drive it, whose eyes we share and who is only looked at, so writers should check whose perspective structures the story and whose is missing.

lessons.title: Comedy structure
lessons.subtitle: Bergson, improv and the sitcom
lessons.summary: Comedy runs on machinery: rigid characters, repetition, inversion and crossed wires, a pattern found and heightened, and a status quo that snaps back so the flaws can strike again.

lessons.title: Bill Nichols
lessons.subtitle: The modes of documentary
lessons.summary: A documentary is shaped reality, a voice made from real material, and its mode, from observational to participatory to reflexive, sets the promise it makes to the audience.

lessons.title: The science of story
lessons.subtitle: What the research does and doesn't show
lessons.summary: Research shows that stories are universal and that absorbing ones persuade, but claims about brain chemistry and science-proven story formulas go well beyond the evidence.
